story:
Peyton ran to the park with Dad. She wanted a cold drink, but her cup was warm. "Yuck," said Peyton. "Warm water is no fun."

Dad had a bag with ice. He put one ice cube in her hand. Peyton yelled, "Cold, cold, cold!" She dropped it fast. It fell into her cup with a plop. The ice cube felt cold when she touched it. That was the trick!

Peyton looked with her eyes. She saw the little ice bobbing. She heard it go clink, clink with her ears. She smelled the sweet apple juice Dad poured in. She took a sip and tasted it with her tongue. "Yum!" she said. She touched the cold cup with her fingers. "More ice, please!" said Peyton. Dad laughed and dropped in two more.

story:

Maeva held the book upside down. She giggled. The fish looked upside down too! The words were all wrong. Dad laughed. "Turn it around." Maeva turned it. Now the fish swam right side up. She opened the front cover first. "Read it again," she said. Dad began, "Once there was a little fish..."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Athena ran to her cubby at daycare. Her bunny toy was not there. She looked under her coat. No bunny. She looked in the toy box. No bunny.

It was winter, so Athena wore her big boots. She searched the reading corner. She lifted the crunchy leaves in the craft bowl. No bunny anywhere. Athena sat down. Her eyes felt hot. She wanted to give up.

Then her big sister came in. Her dad came in too. "Can you help me look?" Athena asked. "Yes," they said. Now three people were searching, not one. Dad looked behind the shelf. Sister looked under the table. Athena looked in the dress-up bin.

Sister lifted a red cape. "Bunny!" she called. Bunny had been hiding under the cape all day. Athena hugged bunny tight. Dad helped her cut a piece of tape. She taped bunny's ear back on.

"More lookers found him fast," Athena said. She waved bye to her teacher. "Come on, bunny. Home time."

story:
Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He wanted a toy fish. The fish was blue and long. Isaiah held it up high.

"I want juice too," he said. "And I want this fish!"

"That is not a fish," said a boy by the toys. "It is a toy."

Isaiah looked at it. It was a toy. He put it back. Then he ran to the food part of the store.

Mama showed him the meat case. "Look, fish," she said. "And look, cow meat. Cows are animals. Dogs are animals too."

"But fish have no legs," said Isaiah. "Fish can't be animals!"

Mama pointed at the fish. It had fins and a tail. It was an animal too!

Then a small dog barked by the door. The dog was real! Isaiah laughed.

"Dogs, cows and fish are all animals," said Mama. "Now let's not forget your juice."

Isaiah got his juice and a cracker. The dog wagged its tail.

"Hi, dog!" said Isaiah.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma's car pulled into the driveway. Amira ran to meet her. Grandma opened the trunk. A big pink suitcase sat inside. "Can I pull it?" asked Amira. "Yes, you can pull it," said Grandma. Amira pulled and pulled. The wheels rumbled on the ground. "What is inside?" she asked. "My clothes," said Grandma. "Guests pack their clothes and things in a suitcase."

Amira thought about that. She looked at the suitcase. How many shirts were in there? How many socks? Grandma unzipped it right there on the grass. Out came one shirt, two shirts, three shirts. Out came a warm scarf and a soft hat. "Why do you bring so much?" asked Amira. "I am staying a whole week," said Grandma.

That night, Amira had an idea. She found her own little bag. She packed one shirt, two shirts, three shirts. She packed her toy sheep. She wanted to be a guest too. In the morning, she rolled her bag to Grandma's room. "Look! I am a guest!" she said. Grandma laughed and clapped. Then she patted the bed. "Come in, little guest. There is room for you and your sheep." Amira climbed up next to her, bag and all.

story:
Leah sat in her car seat. One, two, three toys sat next to her. She had a bear, a bunny and a small red car.

The car went over a deep bump. Leah's bear flew up. The bear came down and hit her baby brother's foot. He began to cry.

"I am sorry," Leah said. "It was a mistake."

Baby brother looked at her. He stopped crying. His face got soft again.

"Can you help me, Mom?" Leah asked. "Please reach the bear?"

Mom smiled in the mirror. She handed the bear back.

"Thank you," said Leah.

Then she made a silly joke. "The bear wanted to swing on the roof!"

Baby brother laughed. The car went on. One, two, three toys, all safe now.

story:
Owen ran into daycare on a windy morning. His hat almost blew off. He had big news. It was his cat's birthday today.

Miss Ada was talking to Ben. "Ben, please pass me the tape," she said. Owen tugged her sleeve. "Miss Ada! Miss Ada!" She held up one hand. "Wait, Owen. I am still talking."

Owen closed his mouth. He watched. Ben gave her the tape. She stuck the paper sun on the wall. Then she stopped. There was a quiet pause.

"Now I am done," said Miss Ada. "You may talk, Owen."

Owen took a big breath. "Today is my cat's birthday!" he said.

"A cat birthday! Thank you for telling me," said Miss Ada. "Can you help me make a card?"

Owen nodded hard. He drew a cat with a party hat. He whispered to the cat in the picture, "Happy birthday."

At snack time, Mia talked about her new shoes. Owen waited. He watched her lips until they stopped. Then he said, "Nice shoes, Mia."

She smiled. "Thank you," she said. Owen smiled too.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Mya stood at the school gate. She held her mama's hand very tight. The gate was huge and red. Behind it, kids ran and laughed.

"Can I run in now?" Mya asked.

"First we wait for the bell," said Mama.

They waited. Ding! The bell rang. The gate opened. Mya ran in.

Inside, the teacher smiled. "Hello, Mya! Sit on the blue mat."

Mya sat down. Then she jumped up. She wanted to run to the toy horse in the corner. It looked so fun!

A boy tugged her sleeve. "We sit on the mat now," he said. "That is a class rule. Everyone follows the rules."

"Rules?" said Mya. "What are rules?"

"Things we all do," said the boy. "Like this one. Sit and listen."

Mya sat back down. The teacher read the rules one by one. One, two, three. Mya counted them on her fingers.

Later, it was play time. Mya ran to the horse. She hugged it and made it gallop. Neigh!

Then the bell rang again. Mya kept playing.

The boy ran over. "Bell means clean up!" he said. "Rule number three!"

Mya put the horse on the shelf. "Rules are not so bad," she said. "Now can we line up?"

"Yes!" said the boy. "You go first."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Ryan ran into the music studio. A big guitar sat on a stand. "Can I play it?" he asked. Miss Kim smiled. "Yes, you can try."

Ryan patted the guitar like a drum. Tap, tap, tap. The guitar made no song. "Why is it quiet?" he asked. Miss Kim said, "Try the strings." She showed him how to strum. Then she said, "You can pluck them too, one by one."

Ryan passed his fingers over the strings. Pluck, pluck. Then he strummed them all at once. Boom! A big, happy sound filled the room. "It sings!" Ryan laughed. His tummy felt warm. He strummed again and again. Miss Kim clapped. "You are a guitar player now, Ryan." Ryan stood tall and proud. "Listen to my song!" he said.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Zayn was a small boy in a big hotel room. He wanted to play plane. "This chair is my seat," he said. Dad sat near him. Dad took the belt from his bathrobe. "Buckle up for takeoff," said Dad. Zayn slid the belt through the loop. Click! "I am buckled," said Zayn. "Buckle up for takeoff," said Dad again. Zayn laughed. "Buckle up for takeoff!"

Then it was time to fly home. On the real plane, Zayn sat by the window. He buckled his seat belt all by himself. Click! The plane began to move. Zayn wanted to stand up. He wanted to look out the window standing tall. "Sit down, buckle up," said Dad. "The plane is taking off." So Zayn sat. The plane went fast. Then the plane went up, up, up! Zayn peeked out the window from his seat. "I can see clouds!" he said. "I am buckled like everyone."

Later the plane came down. "Landing," said Dad. "Buckle up for landing." Zayn held his belt. "Buckle up for landing," he said. The plane touched the ground softly. Zayn looked out the window and waved. "Bye bye, plane," he said.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Arnaud could not sleep. He wanted his favorite cow toy. It was not in his bed. He looked under his pillow. He looked under his blanket. No cow.

Arnaud felt sad. His mouth turned down. Then he heard a bump. It came from the toy box. Arnaud felt a little scared. He held his blanket tight.

Daddy came in. "Let us look," Daddy said. Daddy opened the toy box. Out jumped the cat! The cat had been sleeping on the soft cow.

Arnaud felt surprised. Then he felt excited. "Cow!" he said. He hugged his cow tight. His face made a big smile.

Daddy said, "Look at that happy face." Arnaud ran to the mirror by the door. He made a big smile again. He saw a happy boy looking back.

Then Arnaud made a sad mouth. The boy in the mirror looked sad too. Arnaud giggled. He made an angry face. He made a scared face. The mirror boy copied them all.

Arnaud got back into bed. He held his cow. Daddy tucked him in. "Happy face," Arnaud said softly. He smiled at the ceiling. Then he closed his eyes and went to sleep.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Evelyn ran to the park with Dad. "Good morning," she said to the ducks.

"Good morning?" said Dad. "We woke up this morning. We ate breakfast this morning. Now it is a new part of the day."

Evelyn looked at the sky. The sun was up high. Her tummy was not hungry for breakfast now. It wanted lunch, later.

Evelyn wanted to ride the big girl swing. But Ben was on it. He was going wide, back and forth.

"You can have a turn later," said Dad. So Evelyn waited. She patted the dog. She picked up a stick. She watched Ben's shoes go up to the sky.

Then Ben jumped off. "Now it is my turn," said Evelyn. Dad held the swing. Evelyn climbed on.

"Yesterday this swing was too big for me," said Evelyn.

"And tomorrow you will swing even higher," said Dad.

Evelyn pumped her legs. The swing went wide. "Good morning, birds!" she called.

"Birds eat breakfast in the morning too," said Dad.

Evelyn laughed and swung and swung.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Jules ran to the garden with a little bag of seeds. "Peas!" he said. "I will plant peas!" Grandma made a row in the dirt. Jules dropped the seeds in, one by one. He patted the soil down. Then he watered the seeds. "Grow, grow," said Jules.

Every day Jules came back. Little green leaves popped up. The leaves got bigger. Tall vines climbed up a stick. A fat frog sat by the water can. Jules looked and looked. But where were his peas? He saw no peas at all. "I want peas for my snack," said Jules. He frowned at the vines.

Then Jules saw something long and green. It hung on the plant. "What is that?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "That is a pod," she said. "Pick it." Jules picked the pod. He squeezed it. Pop! It opened in his hand. Inside was a row of little round peas, all in a line!

"Peas!" Jules shouted. "They were hiding in the pod!" He picked more pods, pop, pop, pop. He counted five peas in one. Grandma said they could eat them at home. Jules held his pods tight. "Best garden ever," he said. A red ladybug flew up and landed on a pod. Jules laughed. "You can't have my peas," he said. "They are mine!"

story:
Beatrice went to the mall with her dad. They found the hair salon. Beatrice wanted a haircut, but she also felt a little scared. The scissors looked big and sharp. The hairdresser, Miss Jo, said, "I will be very careful." Miss Jo held the scissors herself. Beatrice sat very still in the big chair.

Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. They stuck to Beatrice's sweater. "Not a bad haircut," her dad said with a smile. Beatrice looked in the big wall mirror. She could see her bangs. She could see her short hair by her ears. But she could not see the back of her head. "I want to see the back," said Beatrice.

Miss Jo did not say anything. She picked up a little mirror. She held it up behind Beatrice's head. Now Beatrice could see the back of her hair in the big mirror. "I see it! It is so short and cute!" said Beatrice. She turned her head slowly. She looked one more time. Then she stuck out her hand for the key-shaped balloon her dad had bought. "Let's go show everyone," she said.

Then he had a question. "Who made up the truck story?" he asked. The store lady smiled. She pointed to the front of the book. "See this name?" she said. "That is the author. activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Leah sat on the classroom rug. Miss Polo held up big letter cards. Each letter had a sound. "B says buh," said Leah. "Buh, buh, bear!"

Then Miss Polo mixed all the cards in a pile. "Can you put them in order?" she asked. Leah picked up the letter M. She looked at the pile. Where did M go? It was hard. There were so many letters.

Her friend Tom grabbed a card and put it way at the end. "No, Tom!" laughed Leah. "That one goes in the middle." Tom stuck out his tongue. "How do you know?"

Then Leah had an idea. She began to sing. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." She tapped a card each time. "H, I, J, K." She tapped and tapped. "L, M! There!" Leah slipped M into its spot, right after L and before N. The song told her where it went!

Tom clapped his hands. "Sing it again!" he said. So they sang the alphabet song together, all the way to Z. Miss Polo smiled at the door. "Now you know your letters, Leah."

Leah hugged the M card. "M says muh," she said. "Muh, muh, me!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Abigail was staying at Grandma's house. It was time to sleep. Grandma said, "Pick two socks from the basket." The room was very dark. Abigail could not see the socks well. She felt two socks with her hands. They felt the same to her. She put them on and went to sleep.

In the morning, the sun came in the window. Abigail looked down at her feet. She saw one red sock and one green sock. She laughed and laughed. "Grandma, come see!" she called. Grandma looked and smiled. "You found a trick of the dark," said Grandma.

The next night, the room was dark again. Abigail had a good idea. She carried the basket to the door. The friendly hall light helped her see. She picked two blue socks. In the morning, both socks were blue. Abigail jumped like she was on a hill of soft grass. "The light helped me," she said. Then she ran to show Grandma her two blue feet.

story:

"May I have a cookie, please?" Elena asked. "Soon," said Grandma. "They are still hot." Just then, the doorbell rang. It was Grandma's neighbor. Her little boy, Tomás, was with her. Tomás was four, just like Elena.

Grandma gave Tomás a cookie on a plate. "Gracias," said Tomás. Elena looked up. That was a new word. "What did you say?" she asked. "I said gracias," said Tomás. "It means thank you. In Spanish, we say it that way." Elena smiled a big smile.

Grandma handed Elena a cookie too. It was cool now. Elena took a small bite. "Gracias," she said. Grandma laughed. Tomás laughed. Then they went out to the yard. The air was warm and soft. A bird swam in the little birdbath. Elena and Tomás played until the sky turned dim. It was getting late. Grandma called, "Time to come in!" Elena waved to Tomás. "Bye, Tomás," she said. "Bye, Elena," he said. "See you tomorrow."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Kinsley sat in her car seat. She held her soft bunny. The car went bump, bump over the road.

"Is the library today?" Kinsley asked. "No, we went yesterday," said Mom. "Yesterday is all done." Kinsley thought about yesterday. Yesterday she got a book with a red truck in it.

"Is today the library?" she asked again. Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is now. We are driving there now." Kinsley looked out the window. Now she saw a cow. Now she saw a big red barn. Now the car went over a bridge.

At the library, Kinsley climbed the little steps to the book shelf. She picked a book about a juicy orange. "Can we read it later?" she asked. "Yes, later at home," said Mom.

"And tomorrow we can come back," said Mom. Kinsley hugged her book. Tomorrow was not here yet. Today was here, and now the cow went moo outside the window.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Henry was at Grandma's house. He had a cold. His nose was red. He wanted to play, but he felt slow and small.

Grandma set out some warm soup. Henry took a sip. Then his nose tickled. "Ah... ah... CHOO!" He sneezed right into his hand.

Grandma gave him a tissue. She wiped his hand. "Watch me," she said. She lifted her arm. She put her nose in her elbow. "When you cough or sneeze, you cover it with your elbow."

Henry tried. He lifted his little arm. He made a cough in his elbow. "I did it!" he said. Grandma clapped.

Then his nose tickled again. Henry moved fast. He put his nose in his elbow. "Ah-CHOO!" This time his hand stayed clean. Grandma smiled big.

Outside the window, the sky was cloudy. Henry drank more soup. Then he coughed once more, soft and small, right into his elbow. "Good job," said Grandma. Henry giggled and held up his arm.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Jules was at home in the kitchen. He had a cold. His nose was red. He sat in his big chair.

Grandma was cooking. "Pancakes today," she said. Jules loved pancakes. He wanted one very much.

But his throat felt scratchy. It hurt a little. He closed his mouth. He thought, if I say nothing, I can still have pancakes. So he stayed quiet.

Grandma set down the pan. "Jules, you look small today," she said. Jules dug his spoon into his yogurt. He did not eat. He looked at his plate.

Then he remembered. "Grandma, my throat hurts," he said. It was a small voice, but she heard.

Grandma put her hand on his head. "Thank you for telling me," she said. "Now I can help you." She made him warm milk with honey. She gave him a soft blanket. Jules sipped slowly. The warm milk felt good in his throat. His heart felt warm too.

Then Grandma put one small pancake on his plate. "When your throat is ready," she said. Jules smiled a tiny smile. He touched the pancake with one finger. "Soon," he whispered, and hugged his blanket tight.

story:
Harper ran to the farm gate. Grandma waved her over. "Time for a game!" she said. "We name our five senses."

Grandma held up a red apple. "Eyes see," Harper said. "I see the apple!" Grandma rang a big bell. "Ears hear!" Harper shouted. She touched a soft sheep. "Hands feel. The sheep is so soft and beautiful!" Then Grandma gave her a warm cookie from the oven. Grandma had done the hot baking herself. Harper took a tiny bite. "My tongue tastes it. Yum!"

"One sense left," said Grandma. "Use your nose." Harper sniffed the cookie. "Mmm, I smell it!" Then she pinched her nose shut with her fingers. She sniffed again. Nothing! She let go and sniffed. The sweet smell came back! "Grandma, come quick!" Harper cried. "Pinch your nose and peek at the cookie smell. It hides!" Grandma laughed and pinched her nose too. "You're right," she said. "I can't smell a thing."

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Layla was at Grandma's house. It was morning. Grandma was baking bread. Layla wanted to help name her five senses. Grandma held up one hand.

"One, eyes. I see the bread," said Layla. "Two, ears. I hear it hum in the oven." Her dad took the bread out with big gloves. "Three, nose. I smell it. Yum!" said Layla. "Four, tongue. I taste a warm bite." Then she stopped. She looked at her thumb. "What about five? Did I forget one?"

She thought hard. Then she touched the soft bread with her finger. "Touching! That is five!" Grandma laughed. Layla counted again on her fingers. "See, hear, smell, taste, touch. Five senses. Five fingers."

Grandma said, "My favorite sense today is smelling." Layla giggled. She sniffed the bread one more time. "Mine too," she said, and took another little bite.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Arthur sat on the big couch. He had a cold. His nose was red and his socks felt warm.

"Can I run outside?" asked Arthur.

"Not yet," said Mom. "Resting on the couch helps your body get better. Here is your bear."

Arthur sighed. He wanted to jump. He wanted to run to the swing. Instead he hugged his bear tight.

Mom brought a blanket. It was soft like a cloud. Arthur pulled it up to his chin. He snuggled down into the cushions.

Then something funny happened. When he rested, his cough got small and quiet. When he sat up fast, the cough came back big. Hmm, thought Arthur. Was the couch doing something?

He stayed very still. He listened to the rain tap the window. He smelled Mom's soup from the kitchen. It smells a little sour, like lemon, he thought, and yummy too.

Arthur rested all morning. He napped with his bear. When he woke up, he wiggled his toes. His nose did not drip. His cough was gone.

"Mom! I feel better!" he shouted. "The couch helped me!"

Mom smiled and kissed his head. "Yes. Resting helps your body get better."

Arthur jumped down. "Can I run now?"

"Yes, you can run now," said Mom, and she held the door open wide.

story:
Victor woke up on his birthday. "A party today!" he shouted. Mom blew up red balloons. Dad hung a big paper chain. Soon Grandma came. Then Ben came. Then Aunt Lily came with a box.

The box was covered in shiny blue paper. Victor could not see inside it. He shook the box. Thump, thump. He squeezed it. It was not scary at all. It was fun! "What is in it?" he asked. "You have to open it," said Grandma. Victor pulled the paper off. Rip, rip! There was a little red truck!

"Now I know," said Victor. "The paper hides the present!" He hugged the box. "Cake time!" called Mom. She cut the cake with a big knife, and everyone sang. Victor held up his new truck. "Beep, beep!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Brielle was at school. It was play time outside. There was a big hoop on the ground. There were little beanbags in a basket. Brielle wanted to throw a beanbag into the hoop.

She picked up a beanbag. She held it with both hands. She threw it. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed in the grass. "Oh no," said Brielle. She got the beanbag. She stood closer to the hoop this time. She threw it again. The beanbag went in! "I did it!" said Brielle. She clapped her hands.

Then Miss Kim, the teacher, rolled a big ball to her. "Now try to catch," said Miss Kim. The ball came and came. Brielle shut her eyes. The ball bumped her arm and rolled away. "I missed it," said Brielle. Her friend Tom shut his eyes too when the ball came. He missed it also. Tom looked sad. His face was not angry, just sad. Brielle patted him on the back.

Miss Kim rolled the ball again. This time Brielle watched the ball. She watched it all the way to her hands. She kept her eyes open. She caught the big ball with both hands! "I caught it!" she said.

A woman at the fence was watching the children. She smiled and waved. Brielle waved back. "Watch the ball, Tom," said Brielle. "Watch it all the way to your hands." Tom watched the ball. He kept his eyes open. He caught it! "Yay, Tom!" said Brielle. They threw the beanbags and caught the ball until the bell rang.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Natalie ran to the baseball field. She wore her red team shirt. It was her turn to hit the ball. She picked up the bat fast.

"Stop, Natalie!" called Coach Ben. "Come get your helmet."

Natalie trotted back. Coach Ben put the helmet on her head. It was blue and a little big. He made the strap snug.

"Now you can hit," said Coach Ben. "The helmet keeps your head safe."

Natalie felt the helmet with one hand. It was hard, like a shell. An ant crawled near her shoe. She watched it for a second, then stepped up to the plate.

She swung once. She missed. She swung again. Miss again. Her friend Milo shouted, "You can do it, Natalie!" Natalie felt a little shy. But she took a deep breath.

The ball came again. Natalie swung hard. Clunk! The ball flew over the grass. "Run, Natalie, run!" said Coach Ben. She dropped the bat and ran to first base. She was safe!

Milo clapped and clapped. "Next time I hit, I will wear my helmet too," he said.

"Good," said Natalie, smiling under her big blue helmet.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Maya stood at the big school door. Her mama held her hand. The hallway was long and empty. "Where is my class?" Maya asked.

A teacher came out. "This way, Maya," she said. "We walk in a line." The children stood one behind the other. Maya saw the line. Each child stood in front of another child. Maya ran ahead to be first. But then she could not see her teacher. She stopped and looked back.

"Come find your spot," the teacher said. Maya walked back. She stood behind a boy with red shoes. Now she could see her teacher. The line moved together, one child after another, all the way down the hall. The teacher smiled at Maya. Maya caught mama's wave at the door.

Inside the room, there was a sandbox. Maya sat down and let the sand run through her fingers. "I like school," she said. The teacher said, "Tomorrow we will walk in our line again." Maya nodded. She patted the sand flat and made a little hill.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Clean-up time came to Natalie's room at daycare. The blocks were in one messy pile on the floor. Miss Jo held up a basket. "We are sorting by color," she said. "All the red ones go together."

Natalie picked up a red block. She put it in the red pile. Then she made a blue pile. Then a yellow pile. Then a green pile. Soon the sun did shine through the window. The colors looked bright on the rug.

Natalie counted her piles. But one block looked wrong. A yellow block sat in the blue pile. "Who put you there?" she asked the block. The block did not answer. Natalie picked it up. She put it with the yellow blocks. Now every block sat with blocks just like it. Sam clapped from the toy corner. He held his doctor kit. "All better," he said. Natalie smiled and set the last basket on the shelf.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Jack waited at the airport. He held a big sign with a heart on it. "There he is!" said Mom. Grandpa waved and walked fast. Jack ran to him and hugged his legs.

At home, Grandpa took out a card game. "I want to go first!" said Jack. He grabbed all the cards. "My turn, my turn, my turn," he said. "But then I never get a turn," said Grandpa. Grandpa looked sad, like an ant with no crumbs. Jack stopped. "You can go first this time," said Jack. So they took turns. Jack went first, then Grandpa went first. They counted, "One turn for you, one turn for me."

They played the game all week. On Friday, Grandpa had to fly home. "Same game next time?" said Grandpa. "Yes," said Jack. "You can go first."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Wesley stood in the pet store. He was very tall for four, but he still held Mama's hand. A small brown puppy looked up at him.

"Can we take him home?" Wesley asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "He is yours."

At home, Mama put food in the puppy's bowl. The puppy began to eat. Wesley wanted to play. He reached for the ball.

"He is eating," said Mama. "We leave him alone now."

Wesley sat on the floor and waited. The puppy crunched and crunched. Soon the bowl was empty. Wesley rolled the ball, and the puppy ran after it in a big circle. Wesley laughed.

Then the puppy yawned. He curled up on his soft bed and closed his eyes. Wesley wanted to pet him. He stopped his hand.

"He is sleeping," Wesley whispered. "I will leave him alone."

He sat very still and watched. The puppy's tail twitched. His paws wiggled. He was running in a dream!

After a while, the puppy woke up. He found Wesley's shoe and gave it a happy chew. "Hey," Wesley said with a giggle. "That's my shoe, not a toy!"

Mama helped him trade the shoe for the ball. Wesley threw it, and the puppy brought it back. "Good boy," said Wesley.

That night, the puppy slept in his bed. Wesley gave him one soft pat on the head. "Good night, puppy," he said. The puppy licked his hand once, just a small good-night kiss.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Mateo sat on a thick carpet at the library. He had a big book of letters. His mama sat next to him.

"A says ah," said Mateo. He patted the letter A on the page. He turned more pages. "B says buh. C says kuh." He kept going. He got all the way to P. "P says puh." He clapped his hands. "All done, Mama!"

A girl sat close by. She was singing a song. "Q, R, S, T, U," she sang. Mateo leaned in and listened. He looked at his book. There were more pages. He turned one.

"V says vuh," said Mateo. "W, X, Y." He went slow. He waited and looked at the letters. The girl sang on.

She sang one more letter. "Z!" said the girl. Mateo turned the last page. There it was. The big letter Z sat at the end.

"Z is the last one," said Mateo. "A is first, and Z is last." He patted the Z, soft and slow.

The girl smiled. "Sing it with me," she said.

"A, B, C," sang Mateo. He sang all the way to the end. "X, Y, Z!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Violet went to the library with her grandma. She wanted a book about a boat. She looked on the low shelf, where the little books hide. Her fingers found a blue book with a boat on the front.

She sat down on the soft rug. She opened the book. But the pages felt wrong. The pictures came in a jumble. A fish came first. Then a storm. Then a little boy at home. "That is all mixed up," said Violet.

Grandma sat close by. "Turn it over," she said. Violet turned the book over. Now the boat picture was at the front. This cover was the front cover. She opened it there.

The first page showed the little boy. Then he got in the boat. Then the fish came. Then the storm. Page by page, the story went in order. Violet turned each page slowly. The paper felt smooth and cool. She heard a page make a tiny flip sound.

At the end, the boy got home safe. That page was near the back cover. Violet patted the back cover and smiled. "It ends at the back," she said. Grandma laughed softly and patted Violet's head. "One more book?" she asked. Violet ran her hand along the shelf, back at the front cover where books begin.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Wesley got to school early. Miss Ana had a surprise. "We will bake bread today," she said. She held the warm pan. Wesley touched the pan. "Ouch, no," said Miss Ana. "Hot pans are for grown-ups." Wesley pulled his hand back.

The bread sat on the wood table. Wesley saw the bread. It was brown and round. He heard it crackle. Then he smelled it. "Yum," said Wesley. "My nose smells it!" Miss Ana gave him a small mirror. "Look at your nose," she said. Wesley looked. He saw two little holes. "What are these?" he asked. "They are called nostrils," said Miss Ana. "Two nostrils!" Wesley shouted. He took a big sniff through both of them. The bread smell came in strong.

Miss Ana cut one slice. She gave Wesley a small piece. He tasted it. "Sweet," said Wesley. "My tongue knows!" He wiggled his toes in his shoes. "My feet can't taste," he said. Miss Ana laughed. "No, feet just walk," she said. Wesley hugged her leg. "My arms hug," he said. Then he took another sniff. Two nostrils, one big smell.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Sienna sat in her car seat. She held her brown bear's foot. But bear's other foot was empty. Her toy bunny was gone.

"I can't find Bunny," Sienna said. Her tummy felt tight.

Mom looked in the mirror. "Don't worry. We will find Bunny. Let's think about our day."

"Retracing your steps means going back to each place you went, in order," said Mom. "We went to the swings. Then the slide. Then the bench. Then the car."

Dad drove back to the park. First they went to the swings. Sienna looked under the swing. No bunny.

Next they went to the slide. Sienna peeked behind the slide. No bunny.

Then they went to the bench. Sienna looked under the bench. There was Bunny! She had been sitting there to eat her snack.

Sienna hugged Bunny tight. "Thank you, Mom. Thank you, Dad," she said.

At home, Dad turned on the lamp. Sienna sat on the couch with Bunny and brown bear. Mom gave her warm milk.

"Now Bunny sleeps with me," said Sienna. She pulled the blanket up to Bunny's chin.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Thomas stood by the big door. The hall was full of people. They were all smiling and talking. He held his grandma's hand tight.

Drums started to boom. People began to dance. Thomas hid behind grandma's coat. "Look," said grandma. "Music and dancing go together. They are part of the party."

Thomas peeked out. His uncle twirled by like a big spinning top. His cousin hopped like a bunny. Thomas giggled. He wished he could dance too.

The music got faster. Grandma held out her hand. "Want to try?" she asked. Thomas took one small step. Then another. Soon his feet were hopping too! He spun and bumped into uncle's big belly. "Oof!" said uncle, laughing. "You squashed me!"

The drums boomed on. Thomas danced and danced until it was late. On the walk home, his feet kept hopping on the street. "Stop dancing, sleepy boy," grandma said. But his toes ticked like a little clock, all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Stella looked out the window. The sky had been stormy last night. Now the backyard was all white. "No school today!" said Dad. "A snow day surprise!"

Stella put on her boots and her red coat. Dad pulled the sled out of the shed. There was a little hill by the fence. Stella wanted to go down fast. She lay on her tummy. "Head first!" she said.

"Not like that," said Dad. He helped her sit up. "Face the way you are going. Hold on here." He stood at the bottom of the hill. Stella touched the sled with both mittens. Down she went, sitting up, facing forward. Whee!

"I want to try again!" she said. Dad watched from his spot. She slid down five more times. Then Stella made a snow cow. It had a carrot for a nose. "Moo," said Dad. Stella laughed and laughed. "One more sled ride," she said. "Watch me, Dad!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Theodore stood in the gym at school. Miss Polly put a hoop on the floor. "Try to throw the beanbag in," she said. Theodore threw it. It hit the edge and fell out. He threw it again. This time it went in. The hoop did not move, but the beanbag stayed. Theodore laughed. One throw made the beanbag land.

Then Miss Polly rolled a big red ball to him. He held out his hands. The ball hit them and bounced out. It rolled away across the floor. Miss Polly rolled it back. Again it bounced out. Theodore wanted to hold it so much. This time he caught it and hugged it to his chest. The ball stayed right there. He did not let go.

"You did it!" said Miss Polly. She clapped. Theodore spun around with the ball still tucked in his arms. Later they sat for a snack. He wore his blue hat and ate crunchy carrots. The big red ball sat by his feet. He hugged it one more time before he went home.
